reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: A partial or complete deficiency of the wall between the coronary sinus and the left atrium, functioning as a form of interatrial communication
It represents the rarest type of atrial septal defect and produces a left-to-right shunt through the coronary sinus into the right atrium
There is a strong association with a persistent left superior vena cava draining to the coronary sinus
When completely unroofed with a persistent left superior vena cava, systemic venous blood can enter the left atrium and cause cyanosis and a risk of paradoxical embolism
The physiology otherwise resembles other atrial septal defects with right heart volume loading
It is frequently part of complex congenital heart disease, including heterotaxy syndromes
Surgical repair reroutes or baffles the anomalous drainage and closes the defect, restoring normal venous return
reference.pathophysiology: An unroofed coronary sinus results from a developmental deficiency of the tissue separating the coronary sinus from the left atrium, so that the two communicate along part or all of the coronary sinus course. This creates an interatrial pathway that behaves like an atrial septal defect, allowing left-to-right shunting and right heart volume loading. The lesion is closely linked to a persistent left superior vena cava that drains into the coronary sinus; when the sinus roof is absent, this systemic venous blood may drain directly into the left atrium, introducing a right-to-left component with desaturation and a route for paradoxical emboli. The defect is often seen within complex malformations, particularly heterotaxy, which shapes the overall haemodynamics.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent left superior vena cava without unroofing
Other causes of right heart volume overload
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography, including agitated saline contrast, to demonstrate the communication and any left superior vena cava
Cardiac CT or MR angiography to define coronary sinus and systemic venous anatomy
Cardiac catheterisation for shunt quantification and pressures
Assessment for a persistent left superior vena cava draining to the coronary sinus
Electrocardiogram for right heart volume loading
Screening for associated heterotaxy and complex defects
redFlags: Cyanosis or documented paradoxical embolism from right-to-left drainage
Signs of significant right heart volume overload or pulmonary hypertension
Association with complex congenital or heterotaxy syndromes
Unexplained systemic desaturation with a persistent left superior vena cava
reference.prognosis: Surgical correction generally has a good outcome, though prognosis is influenced by associated complex lesions; isolated defects repaired before pulmonary vascular disease develops do well.
pitfalls: Labelling the lesion a simple secundum defect and missing the coronary sinus communication
Overlooking a persistent left superior vena cava, which complicates surgical repair
Failing to appreciate a right-to-left shunt and paradoxical embolism risk
Not screening for associated heterotaxy and other complex anomalies
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Surgical correction as the definitive treatment, closing or baffling the coronary sinus communication and redirecting any persistent left superior vena cava away from the left atrium
Timely repair before pulmonary vascular disease develops in the setting of a significant left-to-right shunt and right heart volume loading
Management of the right-to-left component and paradoxical embolism risk when the sinus is completely unroofed with a persistent left superior vena cava
Careful delineation of associated persistent left superior vena cava and systemic venous anatomy to plan the operation
Evaluation for associated heterotaxy and complex congenital heart disease that shape overall haemodynamics and outcome
Attention to infective endocarditis risk and postoperative surveillance within a congenital cardiology service
